title: The Plain of Marathon
text: In 490 BCE, Athenian soldiers met a Persian force on the plain of Marathon. The Greeks used disciplined ranks and knowledge of the ground. Their victory did not end the conflict, but it showed how preparation, courage, and a clear plan can change the course of a difficult day.
context: A concise account of the Battle of Marathon; ancient reports contain uncertain details.
vocabulary: disciplined: trained to act with control
ranks: rows of soldiers
source: Original summary based on standard histories of the Greco-Persian Wars

references.citation: Original summary based on standard histories of the Greco-Persian Wars

title: Two Greek City-States
text: Athens valued public debate, sea power, drama, and philosophy. Sparta organized much of its society around military discipline and service. Neither city represented all Greeks, and neither was simple. Their rivalry reveals how neighboring communities can develop sharply different ideas about citizenship and strength.
context: An introduction to two influential Greek poleis, or city-states.
vocabulary: rivalry: long competition
citizenship: membership in a political community

title: The Roads of Rome
text: Roman surveyors planned roads with firm foundations, drainage, and durable surfaces. Milestones marked distances, while bridges crossed difficult ground. The roads moved armies, officials, letters, and trade. They strengthened Roman rule, yet they also connected distant peoples who exchanged languages, customs, and ideas.
context: Roman roads served military, political, and civilian purposes.
vocabulary: surveyor: one who measures land
durable: able to last

title: The Legend of Cincinnatus
text: Roman tradition says that Cincinnatus left his farm to command Rome in a crisis. After victory, he surrendered extraordinary power and returned to his fields. Historians cannot verify every part of the tale. Romans preserved it as an example of duty, restraint, and service above personal ambition.
context: This is a traditional Roman story rather than a fully documented biography.
vocabulary: restraint: self-control
ambition: strong desire for advancement
source: Original adaptation of a public-domain Roman tradition recorded by Livy

references.citation: Original adaptation of a public-domain Roman tradition recorded by Livy

title: A Harbor for Knowledge
text: The ancient Library of Alexandria sought writings from many lands. Scholars compared manuscripts, studied geometry, mapped the heavens, and argued about language. Much about the library's destruction remains uncertain. Its lasting symbol is not a vanished building alone, but the human effort to gather and test knowledge.
context: The library developed under the Ptolemaic rulers of Egypt.
vocabulary: manuscript: a text written by hand
Ptolemaic: relating to Egypt's Greek-speaking dynasty

title: Hannibal Crosses the Alps
text: During the Second Punic War, Hannibal led a Carthaginian army from Spain toward Italy. The Alpine crossing cost men, animals, and supplies, but it surprised Rome. Hannibal's achievement joined bold planning with enormous risk. It also reminds us that brilliant campaigns can bring terrible hardship.
context: A non-graphic overview of Hannibal's 218 BCE Alpine campaign.
vocabulary: campaign: connected military operations
Carthaginian: from ancient Carthage
source: Original historical summary based on Polybius and modern scholarship

references.citation: Original historical summary based on Polybius and modern scholarship

title: Pictures on Greek Vases
text: A painted Greek vase can act like a small window into daily life. Artists showed musicians, athletes, craftspeople, and families, as well as gods and heroes. Historians compare these pictures with objects and written sources. A vase gives evidence, but it does not tell the whole story by itself.
context: How historians use ancient objects while recognizing the limits of a single source.
vocabulary: evidence: information used to support an explanation
artifact: an object made or used by people
source: Original summary based on The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Scenes of Everyday Life in Ancient Greece

references.citation: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Scenes of Everyday Life in Ancient Greece

title: The Athenian Assembly
text: In classical Athens, male citizens could meet in the Assembly and vote directly on public questions. They heard speeches, considered proposals, and decided matters such as laws and war. This was an important experiment in self-government, but participation was narrow. Women, enslaved people, and resident foreigners could not vote. Athens therefore shows both the power of civic debate and the need to ask who was excluded from it.
context: A balanced introduction to direct democracy and its exclusions in classical Athens.
vocabulary: assembly: a group gathered to make decisions
resident foreigner: a free person living outside his or her home community
source: Original summary based on Smarthistory, The Athenian Agora and the Experiment in Democracy

references.citation: Smarthistory, The Athenian Agora and the Experiment in Democracy

title: The Trial of Socrates
text: In 399 BCE, an Athenian jury convicted Socrates of impiety and corrupting the young. The philosopher had spent years questioning confident claims about justice, courage, and knowledge. His method could sharpen thought, but it also irritated powerful neighbors. Our main accounts were written by followers, especially Plato and Xenophon, so historians compare their purposes and differences. The trial raises hard questions: When does criticism strengthen a city, and when may a city punish speech that it believes is harmful? Its outcome still challenges readers to balance civic duty with honest inquiry.
context: The charges and source problems surrounding Socrates' trial, presented as questions rather than a simple hero story.
vocabulary: impiety: disrespect toward accepted religious duties
convicted: found guilty after a trial
source: Original summary based on Plato, Apology, translated by Harold North Fowler (public-domain edition), Perseus Digital Library

references.citation: Plato, Apology, translated by Harold North Fowler (public-domain edition), Perseus Digital Library

title: Law Written on Twelve Tables
text: About 450 BCE, Romans displayed a set of laws later called the Twelve Tables. The original tablets did not survive, and later writers preserved only parts of their wording. Even so, the tradition matters because citizens could point to rules that were publicly stated instead of known only by officials. The laws protected some procedures while also reflecting an unequal society, including harsh rules about debt and family authority. Written law did not make Rome fair, but it made legal arguments more visible and gave later Romans a foundation to debate.
context: A source-aware account of Rome's earliest famous written law code.
vocabulary: procedure: an established way of doing something
authority: the recognized power to command or decide
source: Original summary based on World History Encyclopedia, Twelve Tables

title: Who Could Become Roman?
text: Roman citizenship began as a status tied to the city of Rome, yet it expanded as Roman power spread. Allies and conquered communities negotiated, demanded, or received different legal rights. After the Social War, laws in the early first century BCE extended citizenship to most free people in Italy. In 212 CE, Emperor Caracalla granted it to nearly all free inhabitants of the empire. Citizenship could offer legal protections and public identity, but it also supported taxation and imperial rule. Rights differed by period, place, wealth, gender, and freedom, so one label did not guarantee equal power. Its history shows that belonging can be both a valuable right and a tool of government.
context: The gradual, contested expansion of Roman citizenship and its mixed political purposes.
vocabulary: legal status: a position recognized by law
imperial: connected with an empire or emperor
source: Original summary based on World History Encyclopedia, Roman Citizenship

title: Reading the Streets of Pompeii
text: The eruption of Vesuvius in 79 CE buried Pompeii beneath volcanic material. Excavated streets, shops, wall paintings, graffiti, and household objects preserve unusual evidence about an ancient city. They reveal commercial signs, political messages, religious practices, and differences of wealth. Yet Pompeii was one place at one moment, not a perfect model of the entire Roman world. Early excavators also removed objects without modern recording methods. Empty rooms may reflect evacuation, decay, or lost finds, and dramatic displays can hide those quieter possibilities. Archaeologists therefore study location and layers carefully, compare Pompeii with other sites, and explain uncertainty instead of treating every discovery as a complete answer.
context: How archaeology produces knowledge from Pompeii while accounting for context and earlier excavation practices.
vocabulary: excavated: uncovered carefully from the ground
context: the surroundings that help explain an object
source: Original summary based on Smithsonian Libraries, Pompeii: The Last Day

references.citation: Smithsonian Libraries, Pompeii: The Last Day
